elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly calls the work 'This systematic review', identifying the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: The research question for this review was ' Are there English-language publications in peer-reviewed scientific journals describing how models have been used to allocate resources for malaria interventions in limited resource settings?' The main aim of this review was to identify and characterize models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in malaria control and elimination settings and to identify their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract/methods explicitly states the review question and main aim/objective.

elements.quote: Editorials, commentaries, opinion papers, conference abstracts, media reports, letters, bulletins, pre-prints, grey literature, non-English language studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were excluded from the search.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly lists excluded study types; inclusion/exclusion criteria are stated in the abstract.

elements.quote: a comprehensive search across PubMed and Embase databases was performed of peer-reviewed literature published from inception until June 2024.
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources (PubMed and Embase) and reports the date range/last search (until June 2024).
The abstract does not mention any methods used to assess risk of bias of included studies.
The abstract does not specify the methods used to present or synthesize the results (e.g., narrative synthesis, meta-analysis) within the abstract text.

elements.quote: The search yielded 2950 records, of which 15 met the inclusion criteria. The studies were carried out mainly in countries in Africa (53.3%)... The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (33.3%) and Case management (33.3%).
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (15) and summarizes study characteristics (geography, interventions) but does not report the total number of participants (no participant counts provided).

elements.quote: The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (33.3%) and Case management (33.3%). The methods used for estimating health benefits were compartmental models (40.0%), individual-based models (40.0%), static models (13.0%) and linear regression model (7%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents descriptive results about interventions and modelling methods and includes counts/percentages of studies, but does not present results for primary health outcomes (effect estimates) or numbers of participants per outcome.
The abstract and paper do not report conducting a meta-analysis; therefore reporting a summary estimate and interval is not applicable.
The abstract does not report comparisons between groups with direction of effect; this item is not applicable based on the abstract content.
The abstract does not briefly summarize limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: The findings highlighted the need for country-specific analysis for malaria control optimization, the use of country-specific epidemiological and cost data in performing modelling analyses, performing cost sensitivity analyses and defining the perspective for the analysis, with an emphasis on subnational tailoring for data collection and analysis for more accurate and good quality results. It is critical that the future modelling efforts account for fairness and target at risk malaria populations that are hard-to-reach to maximize impact.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of results and outlines important implications and recommendations.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.

elements.reason: The abstract (or front matter) provides the registry name (PROSPERO) and registration number.

elements.quote: There is limited evidence in peer-reviewed literature on modelling for malaria optimization in limited resource settings. The country focus of the modelling studies included in the review were not representative of the burden of malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. ... The limited number of modelling analyses for malaria control optimization specific to countries within Africa and Asia is as a consequence of the lack or inaccessibility of country-specific epidemiologic and cost data at the national and subnational levels. This data gap limits future studies within the respective countries, limits the build-up of a critical mass of modellers within these countries, and makes it challenging for policymakers to make an evidence-based informed case to potential donors for future funding.
elements.reason: Text explicitly describes the current state of knowledge (limited evidence, geographic gaps) and important uncertainties/data gaps limiting modelling studies and policy use.

elements.quote: Background Despite advances made in curbing the global malaria burden since the 2000s, progress has stalled, in part due to a plateauing of the financing available to implement needed interventions. In 2020, approximately 3.3 billion USD was invested globally for malaria interventions, falling short of the targeted 6.8 billion USD set by the GTS, increasing the financial gap between desirable and actual investment. Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets. This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: Abstract states the financing shortfall and explicitly explains the need and purpose of the review (to identify and characterise optimisation models for resource allocation in limited-resource settings).
No text in the provided evidence explains whether similar systematic reviews exist, nor cites or contrasts previous reviews or justifies the current review as an update/replication.

elements.quote: Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets.
elements.reason: The review focuses on optimisation models for resource allocation rather than evaluating intervention effects; thus describing an intervention's mechanism of action is not applicable based on the manuscript's stated aim.

elements.quote: All studies investigated WHO-recommended interventions for control or elimination targets (Table 2), such as insecticide-treated nets [10, 11, 16-18, 25, 28, 29, 33-38], seasonal malaria chemoprevention [16, 18, 25, 28, 33, 37], intermittent preventive treatment [16, 25, 28, 37, 38], indoor residual spraying [16-18, 28, 29, 32-38], mass drug administration [16, 18, 29], and diagnosis and treatment through community health workers or health facilities [10, 11, 25, 28, 29, 32, 35-38].
elements.reason: The review summarises modelling studies and interventions considered but does not present or require a logic model for hypothesised causal pathways; given the review's modelling/optimization focus, inclusion of a logic model for complex interventions is not applicable in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: 'The research question for this review was ' Are there English-language publications in peer-reviewed scientific journals describing how models have been used to allocate resources for malaria interventions in limited resource settings?' The main aim of this review was to identify and characterize models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in malaria control and elimination settings and to identify their strengths and limitations.'
elements.reason: The document explicitly states a clear research question and the main aim/objectives of the review, satisfying the requirement for an explicit statement of objectives/questions.

The review addresses identification and characterization of optimisation models rather than effects of interventions; no planned intervention-effect comparisons using PICO or similar are relevant to this review's stated research question.

elements.quote: Each record in the search were included if they met all of the following criteria: (1) Were scientific peer-reviewed journals written in English; (2) Were published before 30th June 2024; (3) Studies were included irrespective of the targeted geographical regions; (4) Studies were included irrespective of the population subgroups; (5) Studies containing an optimization model (mathematical or statistical); (6) All studies with human Plasmodium species; (7) Studies with two or more interventions; (8) Cost data were used in combination with the model outputs; (9) Outcomes/health benefits were clearly stated and/or measured.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists specific study characteristics used to determine eligibility, including publication type/language, date, geographic and population scope, model type, pathogen (human Plasmodium), number of interventions, requirement for cost data, and outcomes.

elements.quote: A narrative synthesis of the study characteristics was performed.

No analyses of heterogeneity are identified as pre-specified or as post-hoc; there is no statement identifying non-prespecified analyses.

The manuscript does not report details of any sensitivity analyses performed. In multiple places the authors state that studies did not perform cost sensitivity analyses and call for performing cost sensitivity analyses in future work (e.g., "they did not meet all the criteria of the quality assessment such as not performing a cost sensitivity analysis"), but the review itself does not describe performing or reporting any sensitivity analyses of synthesised results.

There is no description in the manuscript identifying sensitivity analyses that were not pre-specified. The text notes that included studies generally did not perform cost sensitivity analyses, and recommends performing cost sensitivity analyses in future work (e.g., "not performing a cost sensitivity analysis"), but it does not report any sensitivity analyses conducted by the review nor identify any as non–pre-specified.

No methods are described for assessing risk of bias due to missing results in a synthesis (reporting biases). The retrieved methods focus on data extraction, contacting authors for missing data, and a general quality assessment tool but do not specify any reporting-bias assessment methods.

elements.quote: This manuscript provides a systematic review of existing literature to identify models for malaria control optimization. However, the review has certain limitations, which are outlined below: The review did not include abstracts from scientific conferences or other scientific meetings, potentially omitting important modelling studies conducted by national malaria control programs (NMCPs) to inform resource allocation decisions. And so, although the findings from this review shows that there are relatively few published modelling studies or examples that incorporate cost constraints and describe how to optimize limited budgets, the findings from this manuscript may not fully represent the actual use of models for malaria control optimization worldwide. The absence of these studies from the review limits the comprehensiveness of the findings, suggesting a need for the development of additional approaches to better capture and reflect the full range of modelling activities being undertaken globally.
elements.reason: The Limitations section explicitly describes limitations of the evidence included (e.g., exclusion of conference abstracts and possible omission of NMCP modelling studies), noting how this may limit comprehensiveness and representativeness of the review findings.
